entries.17c198cc5079ed544e366d6162736b3140beda47: <div sID="gen1130" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="35" osisID="Gen.35" sID="Gen.35"/> <div eID="gen1130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1131" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1132" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have three communions and three funerals. I. Three communions between God and Jacob. 1. God ordered Jacob to Beth-el; and, in obedience to that order, he purged his house of idols, and prepared for that journey, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1-Gen.35.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. 2. Jacob built an altar at Beth-el, to the honour of God that had appeared to him, and in performance of his vow, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.6-Gen.35.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. 3. God appeared to him again, and confirmed the change of his name and covenant with him (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.9-Gen.35.13">ver. 9-13</reference>), of which appearance Jacob made a grateful acknowledgment, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.14-Gen.35.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. II. Three funerals. 1. Deborah's, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.8">ver. 8</reference>. 2. Rachel's, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.16-Gen.35.20">ver. 16-20</reference>. 3. Isaac's, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.27-Gen.35.29">ver. 27-29</reference>. Here is also Reuben's incest (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.22">ver. 22</reference>), and an account of Jacob's sons, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.23-Gen.35.26">ver. 23-26</reference>.
entries.2e941428d3d5dace9eb53c6a301c6ef8ec21860b: <div eID="gen1132" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1131" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jacob Summoned to Bethel; Jacob's Journeys towards Bethel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1732.)</title> <div sID="gen1133" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And God said unto Jacob, Arise, go up to Beth-el, and dwell there: and make there an altar unto God, that appeared unto thee when thou fleddest from the face of Esau thy brother. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then Jacob said unto his household, and to all that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, Put away the strange gods that <hi type="italic">are</hi> among you, and be clean, and change your garments: <hi type="super">3</hi> And let us arise, and go up to Beth-el; and I will make there an altar unto God, who answered me in the day of my distress, and was with me in the way which I went. <hi type="super">4</hi> And they gave unto Jacob all the strange gods which <hi type="italic">were</hi> in their hand, and <hi type="italic">all their</hi> earrings which <hi type="italic">were</hi> in their ears; and Jacob hid them under the oak which <hi type="italic">was</hi> by Shechem. <hi type="super">5</hi> And they journeyed: and the terror of God was upon the cities that <hi type="italic">were</hi> round about them, and they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob. <div eID="gen1133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1134" type="x-p"/> Here, I. God reminds Jacob of his vow at Beth-el, and sends him thither to perform it, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">v. 1</reference>. Jacob had said in the day of his distress, <hi type="italic">If I come again in peace, this stone shall be God's house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.28.22">ch. xxviii. 22</reference>. God had performed his part of the bargain, and had given Jacob more than bread to eat and raiment to put on—he had got an estate, and had become two bands; but, it should seem, he had forgotten his vow, or at least had too long deferred the performance of it. Seven or eight years it was now since he came to Canaan; he had purchased ground there, and had built an altar in remembrance of God's last appearance to him when he called him <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.33.19-Gen.33.20">ch. xxxiii. 19, 20</reference>); but still Beth-el is forgotten. Note, Time is apt to wear out the sense of mercies and the impressions made upon us by them; it should not be so, but so it is. God had exercised Jacob with a very sore affliction in his family (<reference osisRef="Gen.34.1-Gen.34.31">ch. xxxiv.</reference>), to see if this would bring his vow to his remembrance, and put him upon the performance of it, but it had not this effect; therefore God comes himself and puts him in mind of it: <hi type="italic">Arise, go to Beth-el.</hi> Note, 1. As many as God loves he will remind of neglected duties, one way or other, by conscience or by providences. 2. When we have vowed a vow to God, it is best not to defer the payment of it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.4">Eccles. v. 4</reference>), yet better late than never. God bade him go to Beth-el and dwell there, that is, not only go himself, but take his family with him, that they might join with him in his devotions. Note, In Beth-el, the house of God, we should desire to dwell, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Ps. xxvii. 4</reference>. That should be our home, not our inn. God reminds him not expressly of his vow, but of the occasion of it: <hi type="italic">When thou fleddest from the face of Esau.</hi> Note, The remembrance of former afflictions should bring to mind the workings of our souls under them, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.13-Ps.66.14">Ps. lxvi. 13, 14</reference>. <div eID="gen1134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1135" type="x-p"/> II. Jacob commands his household to prepare for this solemnity; not only for the journey and remove, but for the religious services that were to be performed, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.2-Gen.35.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. Note, 1. Before solemn ordinances, there must be solemn preparation. <hi type="italic">Wash you, make you clean,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">come, and let us reason together,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.16-Isa.1.18">Isa. i. 16-18</reference>. 2. Masters of families should use their authority for the promoting of religion in their families. Not only we, but our houses also, should serve the Lord, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.15">Josh. xxiv. 15</reference>. Observe the commands he gives his household, like Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">ch. xviii. 19</reference>. (1.) They must <hi type="italic">put away the strange gods.</hi> Strange gods in Jacob's family! Strange things indeed! Could such a family, that was taught the good knowledge of the Lord, admit them? Could such a master, to whom God had appeared twice, and oftener, connive at them? Doubtless this was his infirmity. Note, Those that are good themselves cannot always have those about them so good as they should be. In those families where there is a face of religion, and an altar to God, yet many times there is much amiss, and more strange gods than one would suspect. In Jacob's family, Rachel had her <hi type="italic">teraphim,</hi> which, it is to be feared, she secretly made some superstitious use of. The captives of Shechem brought their gods along with them, and perhaps Jacob's sons took some with the plunder. However they came by them, now they must <hi type="italic">put them away.</hi> (2.) They must be clean, and <hi type="italic">change their garments;</hi> they must observe a due decorum, and make the best appearance they could. Simeon and Levi had their hands full of blood, it concerned them particularly to wash, and to put off their garments that were so stained. These were but ceremonies, signifying the purification and change of the heart. What are clean clothes, and new clothes, without a clean heart, and a new heart? Dr. Lightfoot, by their <hi type="italic">being clean,</hi> or <hi type="italic">washing</hi> themselves, understands Jacob's admission of the proselytes of Shechem and Syria into his religion by baptism, because circumcision had become odious. 3. They must go with him to Beth-el, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.3">v. 3</reference>. Note, Masters of families, when they go up to the house of God, should bring their families with them. <div eID="gen1135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1136" type="x-p"/> III. His family surrendered all they had that was idolatrous or superstitious, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.4">v. 4</reference>. Perhaps, if Jacob had called for them sooner, they would sooner have parted with them, being convicted by their own consciences of the vanity of them. Note, Sometimes attempts for reformation succeed better than one could have expected, and people are not so obstinate against them as we feared. Jacob's servants, and even the retainers of his family, gave him all the strange gods, and the ear-rings they wore, either as charms or to the honour of their gods; they parted with all. Note, Reformation is not sincere if it be not universal. We hope they parted with them cheerfully, and without reluctance, as Ephraim did, when he said, <hi type="italic">What have I to do any more with idols?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.8">Hos. xiv. 8</reference>), or that people that said to their idols, <hi type="italic">Get you hence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">Isa. xxx. 22</reference>. Jacob took care to bury their images, we may suppose in some place unknown to them, that they might not afterwards find them and return to them. Note, We must be wholly separated from our sins, as we are from those that are dead and buried out of our sight, cast them <hi type="italic">to the moles and the bats,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.20">Isa. ii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen1136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1137" type="x-p"/> IV. He removes without molestation from Shechem to Bethel, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.5">v. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">The terror of God was upon the cities.</hi> Though the Canaanites were much exasperated against the sons of Jacob for their barbarous usage of the Shechemites, yet they were so restrained by a divine power that they could not take this fair opportunity, which now offered itself, when they were upon their march, to avenge their neighbours' quarrel. Note, The way of duty is the way of safety. While there was sin in Jacob's house, he was afraid of his neighbours; but now that the strange gods were put away, and they were all going together to Bethel, his neighbours were afraid of him. When we are about God's work, we are under special protection. God is with us, while we are with him; and, if he be for us, who can be against us? See <reference osisRef="Exod.34.24">Exod. xxxiv. 24</reference>, <hi type="italic">No man shall desire thy land, when thou goest up to appear before the Lord.</hi> God governs the world more by secret terrors on men's minds than we are aware of.
entries.89058e8ec3627f4fb11c019b4bad6f141da047f0: <div eID="gen1137" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jacob's Arrival at Bethel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1732.)</title> <div sID="gen1138" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> So Jacob came to Luz, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the land of Canaan, that <hi type="italic">is,</hi> Beth-el, he and all the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he built there an altar, and called the place El-Beth-el: because there God appeared unto him, when he fled from the face of his brother. <hi type="super">8</hi> But Deborah Rebekah's nurse died, and she was buried beneath Beth-el under an oak: and the name of it was called Allon-bachuth. <hi type="super">9</hi> And God appeared unto Jacob again, when he came out of Padan-aram, and blessed him. <hi type="super">10</hi> And God said unto him, Thy name <hi type="italic">is</hi> Jacob: thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name: and he called his name Israel. <hi type="super">11</hi> And God said unto him, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee, and kings shall come out of thy loins; <hi type="super">12</hi> And the land which I gave Abraham and Isaac, to thee I will give it, and to thy seed after thee will I give the land. <hi type="super">13</hi> And God went up from him in the place where he talked with him. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he talked with him, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a pillar of stone: and he poured a drink offering thereon, and he poured oil thereon. 15 And Jacob called the name of the place where God spake with him, Beth-el. <div eID="gen1138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1139" type="x-p"/> Jacob and his retinue having safely arrived at Beth-el, we are here told what passed there. <div eID="gen1139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1140" type="x-p"/> I. There he built an altar (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.7">v. 7</reference>), and no doubt offered sacrifice upon it, perhaps the tenth of his cattle, according to his vow, <hi type="italic">I will give the tenth unto thee.</hi> With these sacrifices he joined praises for former mercies, particularly that which the sight of the place brought afresh to his remembrance; and he added prayers for the continuance of God's favour to him and his family. And he called the place (that is, <hi type="italic">the altar</hi>) <hi type="italic">El-beth-el, the God of Bethel.</hi> As, when he made a thankful acknowledgment of the honour God had lately done him in calling him <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> he worshipped God by the name of <hi type="italic">El-elohe Israel;</hi> so, now that he was making a grateful recognition of God's former favour to him at Bethel, he worships God by the name of <hi type="italic">El-beth-el, the God of Beth-el,</hi> because there God appeared to him. Note, The comfort which the saints have in holy ordinances is not so much from <hi type="italic">Bethel, the house of God,</hi> as from <hi type="italic">El-beth-el, the God of the house.</hi> The ordinances are but empty things if we do not meet with God in them. <div eID="gen1140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1141" type="x-p"/> II. There he buried Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.8">v. 8</reference>. We have reason to think that Jacob, after he came to Canaan, while his family dwelt near Shechem, went himself (it is likely, often) to visit his father Isaac at Hebron. Rebekah probably was dead, but her old nurse (of whom mention is made <reference osisRef="Gen.24.59">ch. xxiv. 59</reference>) survived her, and Jacob took her to his family, to be a companion to his wives, her country-women, and an instructor to his children; while they were at Bethel, she died, and died lamented, so much lamented that the oak under which she was buried was called <hi type="italic">Allon-bachuth, the oak of weeping.</hi> Note, 1. Old servants in a family, that have in their time been faithful and useful, ought to be respected. Honour was done to this nurse, at her death, by Jacob's family, though she was not related to them, and though she was aged. Former services, in such a case, must be remembered. 2. We do not know where death may meet us; perhaps at Beth-el, the house of God. Therefore let us be always ready. 3. Family-afflictions may come even when family-reformation and religion are on foot. Therefore rejoice with trembling. <div eID="gen1141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1142" type="x-p"/> III. There God appeared to him (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.9">v. 9</reference>), to own his altar, to answer to the name by which he had called him, <hi type="italic">The God of Beth-el</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.7">v. 7</reference>), and to comfort him under his affliction, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, God will appear to those in a way of grace that attend on him in a way of duty. Here, 1. He confirmed the change of his name, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.10">v. 10</reference>. It was done before by the angel that wrestled with him (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.28">ch. xxxii. 28</reference>), and here it was ratified by the divine Majesty, or <hi type="italic">Shechinah,</hi> that appeared to him. There it was to encourage him against the fear of Esau, here against the fear of the Canaanites. Who can be too hard for Israel, a prince with God? It is below those who are thus dignified to droop and despond. 2. He renewed and ratified the covenant with him, by the name <hi type="italic">El-shaddai. I am God Almighty, God all-sufficient</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.11">v. 11</reference>), able to make good the promise in due time, and to support thee and provide for thee in the meantime. Two things are promised him which we have met with often before:—(1.) That he should be the father of a great nation, great in number—<hi type="italic">a company of nations shall be of thee</hi> (every tribe of Israel was a nation, and all the twelve a company of nations), great in honour and power—<hi type="italic">kings shall come out of thy loins.</hi> (2.) That he should be the master of a good land (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.12">v. 12</reference>), described by the grantees, Abraham and Isaac, to whom it was promised, not by the occupants, the Canaanites in whose possession it now was. The land that was given to Abraham and Isaac is here entailed on Jacob and his seed. He shall not have children without an estate, which is often the case of the poor, nor an estate without children, which is often the grief of the rich; but both. These two promises had a spiritual signification, of which we may suppose Jacob himself had some notion, though not so clear and distinct as we now have; for, without doubt, Christ is the promised seed, and heaven is the promised land; the former is the foundation, and the latter the top-stone, of all God's favours. 3. He then went up from him, or <hi type="italic">from over him,</hi> in some visible display of glory, which had hovered over him while he talked with him, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.13">v. 13</reference>. Note, The sweetest communions the saints have with God in this world are short and transient, and soon have an end. Our vision of God in heaven will be everlasting; there we shall be ever with the Lord; it is not so here. <div eID="gen1142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1143" type="x-p"/> IV. There Jacob erected a memorial of this, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.14">v. 14</reference>. 1. He set up a pillar. When he was going to Padan-aram, he set up for a pillar that stone on which he had laid his head. This was agreeable enough to his low condition and his hasty flight; but now he took time to erect one more stately, more distinguishable and durable, probably placing that stone in it. In token of his intending it for a sacred memorial of his communion with God, he poured oil and the other ingredients of a drink-offering upon it. His vow was, <hi type="italic">This stone shall be God's house,</hi> that is, shall be set up for his honour, as houses to the praise of their builders; and here he performs it, transferring it to God by anointing it. 2. He confirmed the name he had formerly given to the place (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.15">v. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">Beth-el, the house of God.</hi> Yet this very place afterwards lost the honour of its name, and became <hi type="italic">Beth-aven, a house of iniquity;</hi> for here it was that Jeroboam set up one of his calves. It is impossible for the best man to entail upon a place so much as the profession and form of religion.
entries.4ac313e61a3f43d61c2434803410c1da4a85dcbf: <div eID="gen1143" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Death of Rachel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1732.)</title> <div sID="gen1144" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And they journeyed from Beth-el; and there was but a little way to come to Ephrath: and Rachel travailed, and she had hard labour. <hi type="super">17</hi> And it came to pass, when she was in hard labour, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also. <hi type="super">18</hi> And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Ben-oni: but his father called him Benjamin. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Beth-lehem. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Jacob set a pillar upon her grave: that <hi type="italic">is</hi> the pillar of Rachel's grave unto this day. <div eID="gen1144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1145" type="x-p"/> We have here the story of the death of Rachel, the beloved wife of Jacob. 1. She fell in travail by the way, not able to reach to Bethlehem, the next town, though they were near it; so suddenly does pain sometimes come upon a woman in travail, which she cannot escape, or put off. We may suppose Jacob had soon a tent up, convenient enough for her reception. 2. Her pains were violent. She had hard labour, harder than usual: this was the effect of sin, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">ch. iii. 16</reference>. Note, Human life begins with sorrow, and the roses of its joy are surrounded with thorns. 3. The midwife encouraged her, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.17">v. 17</reference>. No doubt she had her midwife with her, ready at hand, yet that would not secure her. Rachel had said, when she bore Joseph, <hi type="italic">God shall add another son,</hi> which now the midwife remembers, and tells her her words were made good. Yet this did not avail to keep up her spirits; unless God command away fear, no one else can. He only says as one having authority, <hi type="italic">Fear not.</hi> We are apt, in extreme perils, to comfort ourselves and our friends with the hopes of a temporal deliverance, in which we may be disappointed; we had better found our comforts on that which cannot fail us, the hope of eternal life. 4. Her travail was to the life of the child, but to her own death. Note, Though the pains and perils of childbearing were introduced by sin, yet they have sometimes been fatal to very holy women, who, though not saved in childbearing, are saved through it with an everlasting salvation. Rachel had passionately said, <hi type="italic">Give me children, or else I die;</hi> and now that she had children (for this was her second) she died. Her dying is here called <hi type="italic">the departing of her soul.</hi> Note, The death of the body is but the departure of the soul to the world of spirits. 5. Her dying lips called her new-born son <hi type="italic">Ben-oni, The son of my sorrow.</hi> And many a son, not born in such hard labour, yet proves the son of his parent's sorrow, and the heaviness of her that bore him. Children are enough the sorrow of their poor mothers in the breeding, bearing, and nursing of them; they should therefore, when they grow up, study to be their joy, and so, if possible, to make them some amends. But Jacob, because he would not renew the sorrowful remembrance of the mother's death every time he called his son by his name, changed his name, and called him <hi type="italic">Benjamin, The son of my right hand;</hi> that is, "very dear to me, set on my right hand for a blessing, the support of my age, like the staff in my right hand." 6. Jacob buried her near the place where she died. As she died in child-bed, it was convenient to bury her quickly; and therefore he did not bring her to the burying-place of his family. If the soul be at rest after death, it matters little where the body lies. In the place where the tree falls, there let it be. No mention is made of the mourning that was at her death, because that might easily be taken for granted. Jacob, no doubt, was a true mourner. Note, Great afflictions sometimes befal us immediately after great comforts. Lest Jacob should be lifted up with the visions of the Almighty with which he was honoured, this was sent as a thorn in the flesh to humble him. Those that enjoy the favours peculiar to the children of God must yet expect the troubles that are common to the children of men. Deborah, who, had she lived, would have been a comfort to Rachel in her extremity, died but a little before. Note, When death comes into a family, it often strikes double. God by it speaks once, yea, twice. The Jewish writers say, "The death of Deborah and Rachel was to expiate the murder of the Shechemites, occasioned by Dinah, a daughter of the family." 7. Jacob set up a pillar upon her grave, so that it was known, long after, to be Rachel's sepulchre (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1 Sam. x. 2</reference>), and Providence so ordered it that this place afterwards fell in the lot of Benjamin. Jacob set up a pillar in remembrance of his joys (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.14">v. 14</reference>), and here he sets up one in remembrance of his sorrows; for, as it may be of use to ourselves to keep both in mind, so it may be of use to others to transmit the memorials of both: the church, long afterwards, owned that what God said to Jacob at Bethel, both by his word and by his rod, he intended for their instruction (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.4">Hos. xii. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">There he spoke with us.</hi>
entries.538b47b72b8155c116d658b1bea4ecc56510a912: <div eID="gen1145" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Disgrace of Reuben. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1716.)</title> <div sID="gen1146" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And Israel journeyed, and spread his tent beyond the tower of Edar. <hi type="super">22</hi> And it came to pass, when Israel dwelt in that land, that Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine: and Israel heard <hi type="italic">it.</hi> Now the sons of Jacob were twelve: <hi type="super">23</hi> The sons of Leah; Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and Simeon, and Levi, and Judah, and Issachar, and Zebulun: <hi type="super">24</hi> The sons of Rachel; Joseph, and Benjamin: <hi type="super">25</hi> And the sons of Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid; Dan, and Naphtali: 26 And the sons of Zilpah, Leah's handmaid; Gad, and Asher: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Jacob, which were born to him in Padan-aram. <hi type="super">27</hi> And Jacob came unto Isaac his father unto Mamre, unto the city of Arbah, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac sojourned. <hi type="super">28</hi> And the days of Isaac were an hundred and fourscore years. <hi type="super">29</hi> And Isaac gave up the ghost, and died, and was gathered unto his people, <hi type="italic">being</hi> old and full of days: and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him. <div eID="gen1146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1147" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. Jacob's removal, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.21">v. 21</reference>. He also, as his fathers, sojourned in the land of promise as in a strange country, and was not long in a place. Immediately after the story of Rachel's death he is here called <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.21-Gen.35.22">v. 21, 22</reference>), and not often so afterwards: the Jews say, "The historian does him this honour here because he bore that affliction with such admirable patience and submission to Providence." Note, Those are Israels indeed, princes with God, that support the government of their own passions. He that has this rule over his own spirit is better than the mighty. Israel, a prince with God, yet dwells in tents; the city is reserved for him in the other world. 2. The sin of Reuben. A piece of abominable wickedness it was that he was guilty of (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.22">v. 22</reference>), that very sin which the apostle says (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.1">1 Cor v. 1</reference>) is not so much as named among the Gentiles, <hi type="italic">that one should have his father's wife.</hi> It is said to have been <hi type="italic">when Israel dwelt in that land;</hi> as if he were then absent from his family, which might be the unhappy occasion of these disorders. Though perhaps Bilhah was the greater criminal, and it is probable was abandoned by Jacob for it, yet Reuben's crime was so provoking that, for it, he lost his birthright and blessing, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.4">ch. xlix. 4</reference>. The first-born is not always the best, nor the most promising. This was Reuben's sin, but it was Jacob's affliction; and what a sore affliction it was is intimated in a little compass, <hi type="italic">and Israel heard it.</hi> No more is said—that is enough; he heard it with the utmost grief and shame, horror and displeasure. Reuben thought to conceal it, that his father should never hear of it; but those that promise themselves secresy in sin are generally disappointed; a bird of the air carries the voice. 3. A complete list of the sons of Jacob, now that Benjamin the youngest was born. This is the first time we have the names of these heads of the twelve tribes together; afterwards we find them very often spoken of and enumerated, even to the end of the Bible, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.4">Rev. vii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.12">xxi. 12</reference>. 4. The visit which Jacob made to his father Isaac at Hebron. We may suppose he had visited him before since his return, for he <hi type="italic">sorely longed after his father's house;</hi> but never, till now, brought his family to settle with him, or near him, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.27">v. 27</reference>. Probably he did this now upon the death of Rebekah, by which Isaac was left solitary, and not disposed to marry again. 5. The age and death of Isaac are here recorded, though it appears, by computation, that he died not till many years after Joseph was sold into Egypt, and much about the time that he was preferred there. Isaac, a mild quiet man, lived the longest of all the patriarchs, for he was 180 years old; Abraham was but 175. Isaac lived about forty years after he had made his will, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.22">ch. xxvii. 2</reference>. We shall not die an hour the sooner, but abundantly the better, for our timely setting our heart and house in order. Particular notice is taken of the amicable agreement of Esau and Jacob, in solemnizing their father's funeral (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.29">v. 29</reference>), to show how wonderfully God had changed Esau's mind since he vowed his brother's murder immediately after his father's death, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.41">ch. xxvii. 41</reference>. Note, God has many ways of preventing bad men from doing the mischief they intended; he can either tie their hands or turn their hearts.  <chapter eID="Gen.35"/> <div eID="gen1147" type="x-p"/>

entries.1da6047d97817a6ce221fa1550670cdf7b32a5f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv396"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 35</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.35.1-Gen.35.15">Ge 35:1-15</reference>. Removal to Bethel.</title> <div sID="gen585" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv396"/><hi type="bold">1. God said unto Jacob, Arise, &c.--</hi>This command was given seasonably in point of time and tenderly in respect of language. The disgraceful and perilous events that had recently taken place in the patriarch's family must have produced in him a strong desire to remove without delay from the vicinity of Shechem. Borne down by an overwhelming sense of the criminality of his two sons--of the offense they had given to God and the dishonor they had brought on the true faith; distracted, too, with anxiety about the probable consequences which their outrage might bring upon himself and family, should the Canaanite people combine to extirpate such a band of robbers and murderers; he must have felt this call as affording a great relief to his afflicted feelings. At the same time it conveyed a tender rebuke.<div eID="gen585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen586" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go up to Beth-el--</hi>Beth-el was about thirty miles south of Shechem and was an ascent from a low to a highland country. There, he would not only be released from the painful associations of the latter place but be established on a spot that would revive the most delightful and sublime recollections. The pleasure of revisiting it, however, was not altogether unalloyed.<div eID="gen586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make there an altar unto God, that appeared--</hi>It too frequently happens that early impressions are effaced through lapse of time, that promises made in seasons of distress, are forgotten; or, if remembered on the return of health and prosperity, there is not the same alacrity and sense of obligation felt to fulfil them. Jacob was lying under that charge. He had fallen into spiritual indolence. It was now eight or ten years since his return to Canaan. He had effected a comfortable settlement and had acknowledged the divine mercies, by which that return and settlement had been signally distinguished (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.33.19">Ge 33:19</reference>). But for some unrecorded reason, his early vow at Beth-el [Ge 28:20-22], in a great crisis of his life, remained unperformed. The Lord appeared now to remind him of his neglected duty, in terms, however, so mild, as awakened less the memory of his fault, than of the kindness of his heavenly Guardian; and how much Jacob felt the touching nature of the appeal to that memorable scene at Beth-el, appears in the immediate preparations he made to arise and go up thither (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.13">Psa 66:13</reference>). <div eID="gen587" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa130ed8708e62b6864a04598196bbdf1e2666b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv397"/><div sID="gen588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv397"/><hi type="bold">2. Then Jacob said unto his household ... Put away the strange gods that are among you--</hi>Hebrew, "gods of the stranger," of foreign nations. Jacob had brought, in his service, a number of Mesopotamian retainers, who were addicted to superstitious practices; and there is some reason to fear that the same high testimony as to the religious superintendence of his household could not have been borne of him as was done of Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Ge 18:19</reference>). He might have been too negligent hitherto in winking at these evils in his servants; or, perhaps, it was not till his arrival in Canaan, that he had learnt, for the first time, that one nearer and dearer to him was secretly infected with the same corruption (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.34">Ge 31:34</reference>). Be that as it may, he resolved on an immediate and thorough reformation of his household; and in commanding them to put away the strange gods, he added,<div eID="gen588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be clean, and change your garments--</hi>as if some defilement, from contact with idolatry, should still remain about them. In the law of Moses, many ceremonial purifications were ordained and observed by persons who had contracted certain defilements, and without the observance of which, they were reckoned unclean and unfit to join in the social worship of God. These bodily purifications were purely figurative; and as sacrifices were offered before the law, so also were external purifications, as appears from the words of Jacob; hence it would seem that types and symbols were used from the fall of man, representing and teaching the two great doctrines of revealed truth--namely, the atonement of Christ and the sanctification of our nature. <div eID="gen589" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7ce6396c44eeed490f7b632de98a13fef7e879a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv398"/><div sID="gen590" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv398"/><hi type="bold">4. they gave unto Jacob all the strange gods ... and earrings--</hi>Strange gods, the "seraphim" (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.31.30">Ge 31:30</reference>), as well, perhaps, as other idols acquired among the Shechemite spoil--earrings of various forms, sizes, and materials, which are universally worn in the East, and, then as now, connected with incantation and idolatry (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.2.13">Ho 2:13</reference>). The decided tone which Jacob now assumed was the probable cause of the alacrity with which those favorite objects of superstition were surrendered.<div eID="gen590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen591" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jacob hid them under the oak--</hi>or terebinth--a towering tree, which, like all others of the kind, was a striking object in the scenery of Palestine; and beneath which, at Shechem, the patriarch had pitched his tent. He hid the images and amulets, delivered to him by his Mesopotamian dependents, at the root of this tree. The oak being deemed a consecrated tree, to bury them at its root was to deposit them in a place where no bold hand would venture to disturb the ground; and hence it was called from this circumstance--"the plain of Meonenim"--that is, "the oak of enchantments" (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.37">Jud 9:37</reference>); and from the great stone which Joshua set up--"the oak of the pillar" (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.6">Jud 9:6</reference>). <div eID="gen591" type="x-p"/>
entries.bbbd26c26809eff40546f61de15a24e4d1c11b41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv399"/><div sID="gen592" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv399"/><hi type="bold">5. the terror of God was upon the cities--</hi>There was every reason to apprehend that a storm of indignation would burst from all quarters upon Jacob's family, and that the Canaanite tribes would have formed one united plan of revenge. But a supernatural panic seized them; and thus, for the sake of the "heir of the promise," the protecting shield of Providence was specially held over his family. <div eID="gen592" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a4f01ee9dbd602b936a276ced6d03762ad321f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv400"/><div sID="gen593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv400"/><hi type="bold">6. So Jacob came to Luz ... that is, Beth-el--</hi>It is probable that this place was unoccupied ground when Jacob first went to it; and that after that period [Calvin], the Canaanites built a town, to which they gave the name of Luz [Ge 28:19], from the profusion of almond trees that grew around. The name of Beth-el, which would, of course, be confined to Jacob and his family, did not supersede the original one, till long after. It is now identified with the modern Beitin and lies on the western slope of the mountain on which Abraham built his altar (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.8">Ge 12:8</reference>). <div eID="gen593" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7f21a5c9c4ef1e0e3e54ee0382a58a61b513c22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv401"/><div sID="gen594" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv401"/><hi type="bold">7. El-Beth-el--</hi>that is, "the God of Beth-el." <div eID="gen594" type="x-p"/>
entries.676040ff5016dc665de85cffdb40b665503f548e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv402"/><div sID="gen595" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv402"/><hi type="bold">8. Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died--</hi>This event seems to have taken place before the solemnities were commenced. Deborah (Hebrew, a "bee"), supposing her to have been fifty years on coming to Canaan, had attained the great age of a hundred eighty. When she was removed from Isaac's household to Jacob's, is unknown. But it probably was on his return from Mesopotamia; and she would have been of invaluable service to his young family. Old nurses, like her, were not only honored, but loved as mothers; and, accordingly, her death was the occasion of great lamentation. She was buried under the oak--hence called "the terebinth of tears" (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.14">1Ki 13:14</reference>). God was pleased to make a new appearance to him after the solemn rites of devotion were over. By this manifestation of His presence, God testified His acceptance of Jacob's sacrifice and renewed the promise of the blessings guaranteed to Abraham and Isaac [Ge 35:11, 12]; and the patriarch observed the ceremony with which he had formerly consecrated the place, comprising a sacramental cup, along with the oil that he poured on the pillar, and reimposing the memorable name [Ge 35:14]. The whole scene was in accordance with the character of the patriarchal dispensation, in which the great truths of religion were exhibited to the senses, and "the world's grey fathers" taught in a manner suited to the weakness of an infantile condition. <div eID="gen595" type="x-p"/>
entries.6bbcf294ff7eba89e328397ec0fab8b355133648: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv403"/><div sID="gen596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv403"/><hi type="bold">13. God went up from him--</hi>The presence of God was indicated in some visible form and His acceptance of the sacrifice shown by the miraculous descent of fire from heaven, consuming it on the altar. <div eID="gen596" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b9e21bbfff2a2d9ac9272878735b2331cf81ab8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv404"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.35.16-Gen.35.27">Ge 35:16-27</reference>. Birth of Benjamin--Death of Rachel, &c.</title> <div sID="gen597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv404"/><hi type="bold">16. And they journeyed from Beth-el--</hi>There can be no doubt that much enjoyment was experienced at Beth-el, and that in the religious observances solemnized, as well as in the vivid recollections of the glorious vision seen there, the affections of the patriarch were powerfully animated and that he left the place a better and more devoted servant of God. When the solemnities were over, Jacob, with his family, pursued a route directly southward, and they reached Ephrath, when they were plunged into mourning by the death of Rachel, who sank in childbirth, leaving a posthumous son [Ge 35:18]. A very affecting death, considering how ardently the mind of Rachel had been set on offspring (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.30.1">Ge 30:1</reference>). <div eID="gen597" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9d171e9437cb5caec199f3f157ba3e30be662dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv405"/><div sID="gen598" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv405"/><hi type="bold">18. She called his name Ben-oni--</hi>The dying mother gave this name to her child, significant of her circumstances; but Jacob changed his name into Benjamin. This is thought by some to have been originally Benjamin, "a son of days," that is, of old age. But with its present ending it means "son of the right hand," that is, particularly dear and precious. <div eID="gen598" type="x-p"/>
entries.07464230ab3391220f0e7c03ec2ed4f7f800ad25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv406"/><div sID="gen599" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv406"/><hi type="bold">19. Ephrath, which is Beth-lehem--</hi>The one, the old name; the other, the later name, signifying "house of bread." <div eID="gen599" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3e08b023f105bd4a32b05b698787422936bb856: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv407"/><div sID="gen600" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv407"/><hi type="bold">20. and Jacob set a pillar on her grave ... unto this day--</hi>The spot still marked out as the grave of Rachel exactly agrees with the Scriptural record, being about a mile from Beth-lehem. Anciently it was surmounted by a pyramid of stones, but the present tomb is a Mohammedan erection. <div eID="gen600" type="x-p"/>
entries.9555b1979a0d9ed7f3b1d444803e8c9ada0f06ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv408"/><div sID="gen601" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv408"/><hi type="bold">26. Sons of Jacob ... born to him in Padan-aram--</hi>It is a common practice of the sacred historian to say of a company or body of men that which, though true of the majority, may not be applicable to every individual. (See <reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.24">Joh 20:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.13">He 11:13</reference>). Here is an example, for Benjamin was born in Canaan [Ge 35:16-18].<div eID="gen601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen602" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Gen.35.28">Ge 35:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.29">29</reference>. Death of Isaac. <div eID="gen602" type="x-p"/>
entries.0fb7e80721e0d756b14c279332632ef9a9fe16f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv409"/><div sID="gen603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv409"/><hi type="bold">29. Isaac gave up the ghost--</hi>The death of this venerable patriarch is here recorded by anticipation for it did not take place till fifteen years after Joseph's disappearance. Feeble and blind though he was, he lived to a very advanced age; and it is a pleasing evidence of the permanent reconciliation between Esau and Jacob that they met at Mamre to perform the funeral rites of their common father. <chapter eID="Gen.35"/>

entries.cf5dbac2875e57bddc091484f8d8e0af88cab314: <div eID="gen1660" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen1661" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1662" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1662" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1661" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1663" type="x-p"/> Jacob is commanded of God to go to Beth-el, and to build an altar there, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference>. His exhortation to his family to put away all strange gods, etc., <reference osisRef="Gen.35.2">Gen 35:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.3">Gen 35:3</reference>. They deliver them all up, and Jacob hides them in the earth, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.4">Gen 35:4</reference>. They commence their journey, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.5">Gen 35:5</reference>; come to Luz, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.6">Gen 35:6</reference>; build there the altar El-beth-el, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.7">Gen 35:7</reference>. Burial place of Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.8">Gen 35:8</reference>. God appears again unto Jacob, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.9">Gen 35:9</reference>. Blesses him and renews the promises, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.10-Gen.35.13">Gen 35:10-13</reference>. To commemorate this manifestation of God, Jacob sets up a pillar, and calls the place Beth-el, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.14">Gen 35:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.15">Gen 35:15</reference>. They journey to Ephrath, where Rachel, after hard labor, is delivered of Benjamin, and dies, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.16-Gen.35.19">Gen 35:16-19</reference>. Jacob sets up a pillar on her grave, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.20">Gen 35:20</reference>. They journey to Edar, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.21">Gen 35:21</reference>. While at this place, Reuben defiles his father's bed, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.22">Gen 35:22</reference>. Account of the children of Jacob, according to the mothers, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.23-Gen.35.26">Gen 35:23-26</reference>. Jacob comes to Mamre to his father Isaac, who was probably then in the one hundred and fifty-eighth year of his age, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.27">Gen 35:27</reference>. Isaac dies, and is buried by his sons Esau and Jacob, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.29">Gen 35:29</reference>. <div eID="gen1663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1664" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen1664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1665" type="x-p"/> Arise, go up to Beth-el - The transaction that had lately taken place rendered it unsafe for Jacob to dwell any longer at the city of Shechem; and it seems that while he was reflecting on the horrible act of Simeon and Levi, and not knowing what to do, God graciously appeared to him, and commanded him to go up to Beth-el, build an altar there, and thus perform the vow he had made, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.20">Gen 28:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.22">Gen 28:22</reference>.
entries.d36138af7a6a9843867fa694c76cae0f5fc130d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen1665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1666" type="x-p"/> Put away the strange gods - אלהי הנכר elohey hannechar, the gods of the foreigners, which were among them. Jacob's servants were all Syrians, and no doubt were addicted less or more to idolatry and superstition. These gods might belong to them, or, as some have conjectured, they were the teraphim which Rachel stole; but these have already been supposed to be astrological tables, or something of this kind, called by Laban his gods, because by them he supposed he could predict future events, and that they referred to certain astral and planetary intelligences, by whose influences sublunary things were regulated. But it is more natural to suppose that these gods found now in Jacob's family were images of silver, gold, or curious workmanship, which were found among the spoils of the city of Shechem. Lest these should become incitements to idolatry, Jacob orders them to be put away. <div eID="gen1666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1667" type="x-p"/> Be clean, and change your garments - Personal or outward purification, as emblematical of the sanctification of the soul, has been in use among all the true worshippers of God from the beginning of the world. In many cases the law of Moses more solemnly enjoined rites and ceremonies which had been in use from the earliest ages. "A Hindoo considers those clothes defiled in which he has been employed in business, and always changes them before eating and worship." - Ward.
entries.42bff638477109a4c872f3792610547a9720ce18: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen1667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1668" type="x-p"/> Answered me in the day of my distress - Not only when he fled from the face of his brother, but more particularly when he was in his greatest strait at the brook of Jabbok.
entries.d128ab936e9ed8cec20d5bfaf06d383eb7f613fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen1668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1669" type="x-p"/> And - ear-rings which were in their ears - Whether these rings were in the ears of the gods, or in those of Jacob's family, we may rest assured that they were not mere ornaments, but served for superstitious purposes. Ear-rings were certainly worn as amulets and charms, first consecrated to some god, or formed under some constellation, on which magical characters and images were drawn. A very ancient and beautiful one of this kind brought from Egypt, cut out of a solid piece of cornelian, now lies before me. It was evidently intended for the ear, as the opening is too small for any human finger; and it is engraved all over with strange characters and images, which prove that it was intended for a talisman or amulet. It seems to be such a one as St. Augustine describes, Epist. 73, which was suspended from the tip of the ears both of men and women, not for the purpose of ornament, but through an execrable superstition, for the service of demons. "Execranda superstitio ligaturarum, in quibus etiam inaures virorum in summis ex una parte auriculis suspensae deputantur, non ad placendum hominibus, sed ad serviendum daemonibus." See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Gen.24.22">Gen 24:22</reference> (note).
entries.cbf273b6d55886fbcb7ab344f4de3ba14ca07c68: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen1669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1670" type="x-p"/> The terror of God - A supernatural awe sent by the Almighty, was upon the cities that were round about, so that they were not molested in their departure. This could be owing to nothing less than the especial providence of God.
entries.639f241207e40c501676de4c81af08614aa5ab46: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen1670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1671" type="x-p"/> El-beth-el - אל בית אל the strong God, the house of the strong God. But the first אל el is wanting in one of De Rossi's MSS., as it is also in the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, and some copies of the Arabic. The sentence reads much better without it, and much more consistent with the parallel passages.
entries.2486a431088164fdd7785b785c433736efd96ae1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen1671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1672" type="x-p"/> But Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died - She was sent with Rebekah when taken by Abraham's servant to be wife to Isaac, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.59">Gen 24:59</reference>. How she came to be in Jacob's family, expositors are greatly puzzled to find out; but the text does not state that she was in Jacob's family. Her death is mentioned merely because Jacob and his family had now arrived at the place where she was buried, and the name of that place was called Allon-bachuth, "the oak of weeping," as it is likely her death had been greatly regretted, and a general and extraordinary mourning had taken place on the occasion. Of Rebekah's death we know nothing. After her counsel to her son, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.5-Gen.27.17">Gen 27:5-17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.42-Gen.27.46">Gen 27:42-46</reference>, we hear no more of her history from the sacred writings, except of her burial in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.31">Gen 49:31</reference>. Her name is written in the dust. And is not this designed as a mark of the disapprobation of God? It seems strange that such an inconsiderable person as a nurse should be mentioned, when even the person she brought up is passed by unnoticed! It has been observed that the nurse of Aeneas is mentioned nearly in the same way by the poet Virgil; and in the circumstances, in both cases, there is a striking resemblance. "Tu quoque littoribus nostris, <div eID="gen1672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1673" type="x-p"/> Aeneia nutrix, Aeternam moriens famam, <div eID="gen1673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1674" type="x-p"/> Caleta, dedisti: <div eID="gen1674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1675" type="x-p"/> Eet nunc servat honos sedem tunus; ossaque nomen, <div eID="gen1675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1676" type="x-p"/> Hesperia in magna, (si qua est en gloria), signat. <div eID="gen1676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1677" type="x-p"/> At pius exequils Aeneas rite solutis, <div eID="gen1677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1678" type="x-p"/> Aggere composito tumuli, postquam alta quierunt <div eID="gen1678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1679" type="x-p"/> Aequora, tendit iter veils, portumque relinqult." <div eID="gen1679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1680" type="x-p"/> Aen., lib. vii., ver. 1, etc. "Thou too, Cajeta, whose indulgent cares <div eID="gen1680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1681" type="x-p"/> Nursed the great chief, and form'd his tender years, <div eID="gen1681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1682" type="x-p"/> Expiring here (an ever-honor'd name!) <div eID="gen1682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1683" type="x-p"/> Adorn Hesperia with immortal fame: <div eID="gen1683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1684" type="x-p"/> Thy name survives, to please thy pensive ghost; <div eID="gen1684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1685" type="x-p"/> Thy sacred relics grace the Latian coast. <div eID="gen1685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1686" type="x-p"/> Soon as her funeral rites the prince had paid, <div eID="gen1686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1687" type="x-p"/> And raised a tomb in honor of the dead; <div eID="gen1687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1688" type="x-p"/> The sea subsiding, and the tempests o'er, <div eID="gen1688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1689" type="x-p"/> He spreads the flying sails, and leaves the shore." <div eID="gen1689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1690" type="x-p"/> Pitt.
entries.cfe2efcb051ea4a3d9322d340089bbebf5e89fed: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen1690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1691" type="x-p"/> God appeared unto Jacob again - He appeared to him first at Shechem, when he commanded him to go to Bethel, and now that he is arrived at the place, God appears to him the second time, and confirms to him the Abrahamic blessing. To Isaac and Jacob these frequent appearances of God were necessary, but they were not so to Abraham; for to him one word was sufficient - Abraham believed God.
entries.2946a6352db5ff1a58090b6b08476118337c1306: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen1691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1692" type="x-p"/> And God went up from him - This was not a vision, nor a strong mental impression, but a real manifestation of God. Jacob saw and heard him speak, and before his eyes he went up - ascended to heaven. This was no doubt the future Savior, the Angel of the covenant. See <reference osisRef="Gen.16.7">Gen 16:7</reference>.
entries.5a7fdcc2c48090e633abe6530f2959b2a975f32b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen1692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1693" type="x-p"/> A drink-offering - נסך nesech, a libation. These were afterwards very common in all countries. At first they consisted probably of water only, afterwards wine was used; see on <reference osisRef="Lev.7.1">Lev 7:1</reference> (note), etc. The pillar which Jacob set up was to commemorate the appearance of God to him; the drink-offering and the oil were intended to express his gratitude and devotion to his preserver. It was probably the same pillar which he had set up before, which had since been thrown down, and which he had consecrated afresh to God.
entries.9f5640c5548a92aadcd74adc91369e310d83d35e: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen1693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1694" type="x-p"/> There was but a little way to come to Ephrath - The word כברת kibrath, translated here a little way, has greatly perplexed commentators. It occurs only here, in <reference osisRef="Gen.48.7">Gen 48:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.19">2Kgs 5:19</reference>; and it seems to have been some sort of measure applied to land, as we say a mile, an acre, a rood, a perch; but what the exact quantity of the kibrath was cannot be ascertained. Ephrath, called also Bethlehem, and Bethlehem Ephrata, was the birthplace of our blessed Redeemer. See its meaning <reference osisRef="Mat.2.6">Mat 2:6</reference> (note).
entries.3bfcc677599c2c24b60e06edf7de2dcd49743919: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen1694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1695" type="x-p"/> As her soul was in departing - Is not this a proof that there is an immortal spirit in man, which can exist separate from and independent of the body? Of Rachel's death it is said, בצאת נפשה betseth naphshah, in the going away of her soul; her body did not go away, therefore her soul and body must have been distinct. If her breath only had been in tended, נשמה neshamah or רוח ruach would have rather been used, as the first means breath, the latter breath or spirit indifferently. <div eID="gen1695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1696" type="x-p"/> She called his name Ben-oni - בן אני the Son of my sorrow or affliction, because of the hard labor she had in bringing him into the world; but his father called him Benjamin, בנימין the son of my right hand, i.e., the son peculiarly dear to me. So man of the right hand, <reference osisRef="Psa.80.17">Psa 80:17</reference>, signifies one much loved and regarded of God. The Samaritan has Benyamin, the son of days; i.e., the son of his old age, as Judah calls him, <reference osisRef="Gen.44.20">Gen 44:20</reference>; and Houbigant contends that this is the true reading, and that the Chaldee termination in for im is a corruption. If it be a corruption, it is as old as the days of St. Jerome, who translated the place Benjamin, id est, filius dextrae; Benjamin, that is, the son of the right hand.
entries.3816fad7bea43703b5a457e64aa0063cdacda18f: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen1696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1697" type="x-p"/> Jacob set a pillar upon her grave - Was not this the origin of funeral monuments? In ancient times, and among rude nations, a heap of stones designated the burial place of the chief; many of these still remain in different countries. Afterwards a rude stone, with a simple inscription, was used, containing only the name of the deceased, and that of his father. But where arts and sciences flourished, superb monuments were erected highly decorated, and pompously inscribed. It is very likely from the circumstances of Jacob that a single stone constituted the pillar in this case, on which, if writing did then exist, the name, or rather some hieroglyphical device, was probably inscribed. That which is now called Rachel's pillar is allowed, by those who have examined it, to be a comparatively modern structure.
entries.0cad1fb0b47fd6aa0134e6fab74ed50a1d639f4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen1697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1698" type="x-p"/> Tower of Edar - Literally, the tower of the flock, and so translated <reference osisRef="Mic.4.8">Mic 4:8</reference>. It is supposed that this tower was about a mile from Bethlehem, and to have been the place where the angels appeared to the shepherds. The Targum of Jonathan expressly says: "It is the place in which the King Messiah shall be manifested in the end of days." By the tower of the flock we may understand a place built by the shepherds near to some well, for the convenience of watering their flocks, and keeping watch over them by night.
entries.c7d2616c2d1f542af714f2ebf684ac8387f40c83: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen1698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1699" type="x-p"/> Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine - Jonathan, in his Targum, says that Reuben only overthrew the bed of Bilhah, which was set up opposite to the bed of his mother Leah, and that this was reputed to him as if he had lain with her. The colouring given to the passage by the Targumist is, that Reuben was incensed, because he found Bilhah preferred after the death of Rachel to his own mother Leah; and therefore in his anger he overthrew her couch. The same sentiment is repeated by Jonathan, and glanced at by the Jerusalem Targum, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.4">Gen 49:4</reference>. Could this view of the subject be proved to be correct, both piety and candour would rejoice. <div eID="gen1699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1700" type="x-p"/> And Israel heard it - Not one word is added farther in the Hebrew text; but a break is left in the verse, opposite to which there is a Masoretic note, which simply states that there is a hiatus in the verse. This hiatus the Septuagint has thus supplied: και πονηρον εφανη εναντιον αυτον, and it appeared evil in his sight. <div eID="gen1700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1701" type="x-p"/> Now the sons of Jacob were twelve - Called afterwards the twelve patriarchs, because they became heads or chiefs of numerous families or tribes, <reference osisRef="Act.7.8">Act 7:8</reference>; and the people that descended from them are called the twelve tribes, <reference osisRef="Act.26.7">Act 26:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jam.1.1">Jam 1:1</reference>. Twelve princes came from Ishmael, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.16">Gen 25:16</reference>, who were heads of families and tribes. And in reference to the twelve patriarchs, our Lord chose twelve apostles. Strictly speaking, there were thirteen tribes among the Hebrews, as Ephraim and Manasses were counted for tribes, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.5">Gen 48:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.6">Gen 48:6</reference>; but the Scripture in naming them, says Mr. Ainsworth, usually sets down but twelve, omitting the name now of one, then of another, as may in sundry places be observed, Deuteronomy 33; Ezekiel 48; Revelation 12, etc.
entries.4a884acf6dc8fdba1043bdf4a2ad56980d6064ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen1701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1702" type="x-p"/> The sons of Leah - The children are arranged under their respective mothers, and not in order of their birth.
entries.1329f659d0097d46524e66eed487175b32fbc867: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen1702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1703" type="x-p"/> Born to him in Padan-aram - i.e., all but Benjamin was born in Canaan, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.16">Gen 35:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.17">Gen 35:17</reference>. <div eID="gen1703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1704" type="x-p"/> It is well known that Padan-aram is the same as Mesopotamia, and hence the Septuagint translate Μεσοποταμια της Συριας, Mesopotamia of Syria. The word signifies between the two rivers, from μεσος the midst, and ποταμος, a river. It is situated between the Euphrates and Tigris, having Assyria on the east, Arabia Deserta, with Babylonia, on the south, Syria on the west, and Armenia on the north. It is now the province of Diarbek, in Asiatic Turkey, and is sometimes called Maverannahar, the country beyond the river; and Aram Naharaim, Aram or Syria of the two rivers.
entries.cc309f185bbed0fc99b752ba0b53e0458c7989fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen1704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1705" type="x-p"/> The city of Arbah, (which is Hebron) - See <reference osisRef="Gen.23.2">Gen 23:2</reference>. It has been conjectured that Jacob must have paid a visit to his father before this time, as previously to this he had been some years in Canaan; but now, as he was approaching to his end, Jacob is supposed to have gone to live with and comfort him in his declining days.
entries.96d740a412e25a8eee45de55f309ebd3fbba6763: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen1705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1706" type="x-p"/> Isaac gave up the ghost - and was gathered unto his people - See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Gen.25.8">Gen 25:8</reference> (note). <div eID="gen1706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1707" type="x-p"/> Esau and Jacob buried him - See <reference osisRef="Gen.25.9">Gen 25:9</reference>. Esau, as we have seen Genesis 33, was thoroughly reconciled to his brother Jacob, and now they both join in fraternal and filial affection to do the last kind office to their amiable father. It is generally allowed that the death of Isaac is mentioned here out of its chronological order, as several of the transactions mentioned in the succeeding chapters, especially 37 and 38, must have happened during his life; but that the history of Joseph might not be disturbed, his death is anticipated in this place. It is supposed that he lived at least twelve years after Joseph was sold into Egypt. <div eID="gen1707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1708" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains several subjects which are well worthy of the reader's most serious attention. <div eID="gen1708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1709" type="x-p"/> 1. That such a family as that of Jacob should have had false gods in it, is a matter not less astonishing than real: and suppose that we allow, as is very probable, that their images and rings were got from strangers, the Syrians and the Shechemites, yet their being tolerated in the family, though it is probable this was for a very short time, cannot be easily accounted for. It is true the Law was not then given, and the unity of God not so particularly taught as it was afterwards. Besides, we have already seen that certain superstitions were compatible in those early times with general sincerity and attachment to the truth; those times and acts of ignorance were winked at, till superior light shone upon the world. Between many of the practices of Laban's family and those of the surrounding heathenish tribes, there might have been but little difference; and this was probably the reason why Dinah could so readily mix with the daughters of the land, <reference osisRef="Gen.34.1">Gen 34:1</reference>, which led to the fatal consequences already reviewed. Sin is like the letting out of water - when once a breach is made in the dyke, the stream becomes determined to a wrong course, and its progress is soon irresistible. Had not Jacob put away these strange gods, the whole family might have been infected with idolatry. This saying of one of the ancients is good, Vitia transmittit ad posteros, qui praesentibus culpis ignoscit - Seneca. "He who is indulgent to present offenses, transmits sin to posterity." The first motions of it should be firmly resisted; after struggles are too often fruitless. <div eID="gen1709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1710" type="x-p"/> 2. The doctrine of a particular and especial providence has another proof in this chapter. After the sanguinary conduct of Jacob's sons, is it not surprising that the neighboring tribes did not join together and extirpate the whole family? And so they certainly would, had not the terror of God fallen upon them, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.5">Gen 35:5</reference>. Jacob and the major part of his family were innocent of this great transgression; and on the preservation of their lives, the accomplishment of great events depended: therefore God watches over them, and shields them from the hands of their enemies. <div eID="gen1710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1711" type="x-p"/> 3. The impatience and fate of the amiable Rachel, who can read of without deploring? Give me children, said she, or else I die, <reference osisRef="Gen.30.1">Gen 30:1</reference>. Her desire was granted, and her death was the consequence! God's way is ever best. We know not what we ask, nor what we ought to ask, and therefore often ask amiss when we petition for such secular things as belong to the dispensations of God's providence. For things of this kind we have no revealed directory; and when we ask for them, it should be with the deepest submission to the Divine will, as God alone knows what is best for us. With respect to the soul, every thing is clearly revealed, so that we may ask and receive, and have a fullness of joy; but as to our bodies, there is much reason to fear that the answer of our petitions would be, in numerous cases, our inevitable destruction. How many prayers does God in mercy shut out! <div eID="gen1711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1712" type="x-p"/> 4. The transgression of Reuben, of whatsoever kind, was marked, not only by the displeasure of his father, but by that of God also; see <reference osisRef="Gen.49.4">Gen 49:4</reference>. It brought a curse upon him, and he forfeited thereby the right of primogeniture and the priesthood: the first was given to Judah, the second to Levi. Is it not in reference to this that our Lord addresses these solemn words to the angel of the Church of Philadelphia: Behold, I come quickly; hold that fast which thou hast, that No Man Take Thy Crown? A man, by sowing a grain of forbidden sweets, may reap an abundant harvest of eternal wretchedness. Reader, let not sin rob thee of the kingdom of God. <div eID="gen1712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1713" type="x-p"/> 5. Here we have the death of Isaac recorded: most that can be said of his character has been already anticipated, see Genesis 22, etc. He appears to have been generally pious, deeply submissive and obedient. He was rather an amiable and good, than a great and useful, man. If compared with his son Jacob, in the early part of their lives, he appears to great advantage, as possessing more sincerity and more personal piety. But if compared with his father Abraham, O, what a falling off is here! Abraham is the most perfect character under the Old Testament, and even under the New he has no parallel but St. Paul. Isaac, though falling far short of his father's excellences, will ever remain a pattern of piety and filial obedience.  <chapter eID="Gen.35"/> <div eID="gen1713" type="x-p"/>

entries.3867d318bb10f35b43340f07b67f0960e57cb88d: <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1-Gen.35.7">Gen 35:1-7</reference> <hi type="italic">Journey to Bethel</hi>. - Jacob had allowed ten years to pass since his return from Mesopotamia, without performing the vow which he made at Bethel when fleeing from Esau (Gen 28:20.), although he had recalled it to mind when resolving to return (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.13">Gen 31:13</reference>), and had also erected an altar in Shechem to the “God of Israel” (<reference osisRef="Gen.33.20">Gen 33:20</reference>). He was now directed by God (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference>) to go to Bethel, and there build an altar to the God who had appeared to him on his flight from Esau. This command stirred him up to perform what had been neglected, viz., to put away from his house the strange gods, which he had tolerated in weak consideration for his wives, and which had no doubt occasioned the long neglect, and to pay to God the vow that he had made in the day of his trouble. He therefore commanded his house (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.2">Gen 35:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.3">Gen 35:3</reference>), i.e., his wives and children, and “<hi type="italic">all that were with him,</hi>” i.e., his men and maid-servants, to put away the strange gods, to purify themselves, and wash their clothes. He also buried “all the strange gods,” i.e., Rachel’s teraphim (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.19">Gen 31:19</reference>), and whatever other idols there were, with the earrings which were worn as amulets and charms, “<hi type="italic">under the terebinth at Shechem,</hi>” probably the very tree under which Abraham once pitched his tent (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Gen 12:6</reference>), and which was regarded as a sacred place in Joshua’s time (vid., <reference osisRef="Josh.24.26">Jos 24:26</reference>, though the pointing is אלּה there). The burial of the idols was followed by purification through the washing of the body, as a sign of the purification of the heart from the defilement of idolatry, and by the putting on of clean and festal clothes, as a symbol of the sanctification and elevation of the heart to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.23">Jos 24:23</reference>). This decided turning to the Lord was immediately followed by the blessing of God. When they left Shechem a “<hi type="italic">terror of God,</hi>” i.e., a supernatural terror, “<hi type="italic">came upon the cities round about,</hi>” so that they did not venture to pursue the sons of Jacob on account of the cruelty of Simeon and Levi (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.5">Gen 35:5</reference>). Having safely arrived in Bethel, Jacob built an altar, which he called <hi type="italic">El Bethel</hi> (God of Bethel) in remembrance of the manifestation of God on His flight from Esau.
entries.856e2e5e28000b007c14afb95ada7f089b8559a9: <reference osisRef="Gen.35.8">Gen 35:8</reference> <div eID="gen412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen413" type="x-p"/> There <hi type="italic">Deborah</hi>, Rebekah’s nurse, died, and was buried below Bethel under an oak, which was henceforth called the “oak of weeping,” a mourning oak, from the grief of Jacob’s house on account of her death. Deborah had either been sent by Rebekah to take care of her daughters-in-law and grandsons, or had gone of her own accord into Jacob’s household after the death of her mistress. The mourning at her death, and the perpetuation of her memory, are proofs that she must have been a faithful and highly esteemed servant in Jacob’s house.
entries.1c5e57dcb9fff91fe2ecaa0df6cf2fb4c59f0964: <reference osisRef="Gen.35.9-Gen.35.15">Gen 35:9-15</reference> <div eID="gen413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen414" type="x-p"/> The Fresh Revelation at Bethel. - After Jacob had performed his vow by erecting the altar at Bethel, God appeared to him again there (“<hi type="italic">again,</hi>” referring to Gen 28), “<hi type="italic">on his coming out of Padan-Aram,</hi>” as He had appeared to him 30 years before on his journey thither, - though it was then in a dream, now by daylight in a visible form (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.35.13">Gen 35:13</reference>, “<hi type="italic">God went up from him</hi>”). The gloom of that day of fear had now brightened into the clear daylight of salvation. This appearance was the answer, which God gave to Jacob on his acknowledgement of Him; and its reality is thereby established, in opposition to the conjecture that it is merely a legendary repetition of the previous vision.<note placement="foot">This conjecture derives no support from the fact that the manifestations of God are ascribed to <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference> and Gen 35:9., although the whole chapter treats of the display of mercy by the covenant God, i.e., <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>. For the occurrence of <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference> may be explained, partly from the antithesis of God and man (because <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi>, the man, had neglected to redeem his vow, it was necessary that he should be reminded of it by God), and partly from the fact that there is no allusion to any <hi type="italic">appearance</hi> of God, but the words “God said” are to be understood, no doubt, as relating to an inward communication. The use of <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in Gen 35:9. follows naturally from the injunction of <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference>; and there was the less necessity for an express designation of the God appearing as <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, because, on the one hand, the object of this appearance was simply to renew and confirm the former appearance of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> (Gen 28:12.), and on the other hand, the title assumed in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.11">Gen 35:11</reference>, <hi type="italic">El Shaddai</hi>, refers to <reference osisRef="Gen.27.1">Gen 27:1</reference>, where <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> announces Himself to Abram as <hi type="italic">El Shaddai</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen415" type="x-p"/> The former theophany had promised to Jacob divine protection in a foreign land and restoration to his home, on the ground of his call to be the bearer of the blessings of salvation. This promise God had fulfilled, and Jacob therefore performed his vow. On the strength of this, God now confirmed to him the name of Israel, which He had already given him in <reference osisRef="Gen.32.28">Gen 32:28</reference>, and with it the promised of a numerous seed and the possession of Canaan, which, so far as the form and substance are concerned, points back rather to <reference osisRef="Gen.17.6">Gen 17:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.17.8">Gen 17:8</reference> than to <reference osisRef="Gen.28.13-Gen.28.14">Gen 28:13-14</reference>, and for the fulfilment of which, commencing with the birth of his sons and his return to Canaan, and stretching forward to the most remote future, the name of <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> was to furnish him with a pledge. - Jacob alluded to this second manifestation of God at Bethel towards the close of his life (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.3-Gen.48.4">Gen 48:3-4</reference>); and Hosea (Hos 12:4) represents it as the result of his wrestling with God. The remembrance of this appearance Jacob transmitted to his descendants by erecting a memorial stone, which he not only anointed with oil like the former one in <reference osisRef="Gen.28.17">Gen 28:17</reference>, but consecrated by a drink-offering and by the renewal of the name Bethel.
entries.dea93c00d5278f181e1eb2884d7a857d64f87cd7: <reference osisRef="Gen.35.16-Gen.35.20">Gen 35:16-20</reference> <div eID="gen415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen416" type="x-p"/> Birth of Benjamin and Death of Rachel. - Jacob’s departure from Bethel was not in opposition to the divine command, “dwell there” (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference>). For the word שׁב does not enjoin a permanent abode; but, when taken in connection with what follows, “make there an altar,” it merely directs him to stay there and perform his vow. As they were travelling forward, Rachel was taken in labour not far from Ephratah. הארץ כּברת is a space, answering probably to the Persian parassang, though the real meaning of כּברה is unknown. The birth was a difficult one. בּלדתּהּ תּקשׁ: she had difficulty in her labour (instead of <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> we find <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.17">Gen 35:17</reference> with the same signification). The midwife comforted her by saying: “<hi type="italic">Fear not, for this also is to thee a son,</hi>” - a wish expressed by her when Joseph was born (<reference osisRef="Gen.30.24">Gen 30:24</reference>).
